reviews.text: 🛕 Yonghe Temple (Lama Temple), Beijing Lama Temple, also known as Yonghe Temple, is one of the most peaceful and spiritually significant places to visit in Beijing. It is a comfortable and calming place for prayer, reflection, and gratitude. Today is the first day of the Lunar calendar in 2026, a very special and auspicious day. Many people come here to pray for health, prosperity, and good fortune for the new year. When you enter, you purchase an admission ticket for RMB 25. After entering, visitors can receive incense sticks to offer prayers and express gratitude according to their own beliefs. The atmosphere is respectful and serene, especially on important lunar dates. ⸻ 🏯 History of Lama Temple • The temple was originally built in 1694 during the Qing Dynasty as a residence for Prince Yong (who later became the Yongzheng Emperor). • In 1744, it was converted into a Tibetan Buddhist monastery and became one of the most important Tibetan Buddhist temples outside Tibet. • It is known for combining Han Chinese and Tibetan architectural styles, creating a unique cultural blend. • One of its most famous features is the 18-meter tall Maitreya Buddha statue, carved from a single piece of white sandalwood. This statue is listed in the Guinness World Records. Today, Lama Temple remains an active place of worship for Tibetan Buddhism and a cultural landmark in Beijing. It represents harmony between different Buddhist traditions and is considered a powerful place for spiritual blessings.

My first attempt? A total failure—blocked by a sea of people at the entrance. But on my second visit to Beijing, mission accomplished! I finally entered this ancient imperial palace with its yellow roofs, the vibrant heart of Tibetan Buddhism outside of Tibet. Inside, time seems to stop. The scent of incense, the whispers of mantras, the colossal sandalwood Buddha statue… A total immersion in the sacred. Personal discovery: here, you visit from south to north, from the monumental gates to the main sanctuary, following a symbolic axis that leads from the secular world to the spiritual heart. I was lost without even realizing it, caught in this millennia-old logic! A haven of peace in the heart of Beijing, where imperial history and living devotion meet. If you go, be patient—and let yourself be carried by its ancient flow.

The Lama Temple (Yonghe Temple) in Beijing is one of the city’s most atmospheric and culturally rich sites, perfect for anyone wanting a break from the urban buzz and a window into traditional Tibetan Buddhism. This beautifully preserved temple complex combines elegant Chinese and Tibetan architectural styles, with vibrant colors, ornate roofs, and peaceful courtyards that invite slow exploration. Inside, the highlight is the awe-inspiring 18-meter statue of Maitreya Buddha carved from a single piece of sandalwood, which draws both visitors and worshippers alike and creates a powerful sense of presence. Many people enjoy the serene ritual of incense burning and the scent of smoke lingering through the halls, adding to the immersive experience. It’s still an active place of worship, so you’ll see monks and locals praying alongside tourists, which gives the visit an authentic feel. The temple is easily reached by subway and fits well into a half-day of cultural sightseeing in Beijing

The Lama Temple, known locally as Yonghe Gong (雍和宫), stands as one of Beijing's most magnificent and culturally significant Buddhist monasteries. Located in the northeastern part of the city, this active Tibetan Buddhist temple offers visitors a rare glimpse into both imperial Chinese history and living religious practice. The temple's origins are deeply intertwined with China's imperial past. Built in 1694 during the Qing Dynasty, it originally served as the residence of Prince Yong, who would later become the Yongzheng Emperor. After his ascension to the throne in 1722, the complex was converted into a lamasery in 1744 by his son, the Qianlong Emperor. This transformation made it one of the most important centers of Tibetan Buddhism outside of Tibet. The temple complex exemplifies traditional Chinese palatial architecture combined with Tibetan Buddhist influences. Its layout follows a traditional north-south axis, with five main halls connected by courtyards. The buildings feature the characteristic yellow roof tiles reserved for imperial structures, while the interiors showcase intricate Tibetan-style decorations, thangka paintings, and Buddhist statuary. The most famous treasure is the towering 18-meter (59-foot) statue of Maitreya Buddha carved from a single piece of white sandalwood, housed in the Wanfu Pavilion. This impressive sculpture is a gift from the seventh Dalai Lama and remains one of the temple's most photographed features. Unlike many historical sites in Beijing, Lama Temple remains an active place of worship. Monks in traditional robes can be seen throughout the complex, and the air is thick with incense smoke from devotees' offerings. This living quality gives the temple an authentic spiritual atmosphere that purely historical sites cannot match. Visitors should be respectful of worshippers and observe proper temple etiquette. The temple is remarkably accessible for tourists while maintaining its religious function. English signage helps explain the significance of different halls and artifacts, though the explanations can be somewhat brief. The complex takes about 1-2 hours to explore thoroughly, though those interested in Buddhist art and architecture could easily spend longer. The surrounding Yonghe Lamasery Street has developed into a charming area with shops selling Buddhist items, traditional crafts, and local snacks, adding to the overall cultural experience. The temple can get quite crowded, especially on weekends and Buddhist holidays. Early morning visits offer a more peaceful experience and better photo opportunities. The entrance fee is modest, and the location is easily accessible via Beijing's subway system (Yonghe Gong station on Line 2 and Line 5). Lama Temple successfully bridges the gap between museum and sanctuary, offering cultural tourists meaningful insights into Tibetan Buddhism while serving as a genuine place of worship. Its combination of imperial grandeur, religious authenticity, and cultural accessibility makes it an essential stop for anyone interested in understanding Beijing's diverse spiritual heritage. Whether you're drawn by history, architecture, or spirituality, Yonghe Temple delivers a memorable and enriching experience.

The Yonghe Temple, or Palace of Peace and Harmony, is better known to the general public as the Lama Temple. In 1694, a former residence of Ming Dynasty court eunuchs was converted into the residence of Yinzhen, the future Crown Prince Yong, who moved in in 1703. In 1722, when Crown Prince Yong succeeded his father as the Yongzheng Emperor, the residence's name was changed to the "Palace of Peace and Harmony." The Qianlong Emperor, who was born here in 1711, granted the residence imperial status, hence the yellow, "imperial" roof tiles on the Lama Temple's buildings. In 1744, the emperor decreed that the palace become a lamasery, a Tibetan monastery, and due to the influx of Tibetan Buddhist monks, the temple became the national center of lama administration. Since 1793, with the foundation of the Golden Urn, the Yonghe Temple also became a place for the Qing dynasty (and later the CCP) to exert control over the Tibetan and Mongolian lama reincarnations. In 1929, the temple was the site of the Beijing Revolt, an armed mutiny against the Nationalist government. Twenty years later, after the proclamation of the People's Republic of China, the monastery was closed and did not reopen for another 32 years. Thanks to the intervention of Zhou Enlai, the temple survived the Cultural Revolution and opened its doors to the public in 1981. Today, it is once again a functioning lamasery, inhabited and administered by monks of the Gelug School. Highlights of the Lama Temple are the Falun Dian and the Wanfu Ge. The Falun Dian is the hall built in 1694 in honor of Tsongkapa, the founder of the Gelug Order (also known as the Yellow Caps), and its architecture most closely resembles a Tibetan temple. The Wanfu Ge, dating from 1750, houses the 26-meter-tall Buddha statue that Kälsang Gyatso, the Seventh Dalai Lama, presented to the Qianlong Emperor. Allow a few hours to visit this temple complex; it's definitely worth it!

The Yonghe Temple (Chinese: 雍和宫, "Palace of Peace and Harmony"), also known as the Yonghe Lamasery, or popularly as the Lama Temple, is a temple and monastery of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism located in Dongcheng District, Beijing, China. The building and artwork of the temple is a combination of Han Chinese and Tibetan styles. Building work on the Yonghe Temple started in 1694 during the Qing dynasty on the site where originally stood an official residence for court eunuchs of the previous dynasty. It was then converted into the residence of Yinzhen (Prince Yong), the fourth son of the Kangxi Emperor. After Prince Yong ascended the throne as the Yongzheng Emperor in 1722, half of the building was converted into a lamasery, a monastery for monks of Tibetan Buddhism. The other half remained an imperial palace. After the Yongzheng Emperor's death in 1735, his coffin was placed in the temple. The Qianlong Emperor, who succeeded the Yongzheng Emperor, gave the temple imperial status signified by having its turquoise tiles replaced with yellow tiles which were reserved for the emperor. Subsequently, the monastery became a residence for large numbers of Tibetan Buddhist monks from Mongolia and Tibet, and so the Yonghe Lamasery became the national centre of Lama administration. The temple was the site of an armed revolt against the Chinese Nationalist government in 1929. After the Chinese Civil War ended in 1949, the temple was declared a national monument and closed for the following 32 years.[2] It is said to have survived the Cultural Revolution due to the intervention of Premier Zhou Enlai. Reopened to the public in 1981, it is today both a functioning temple and highly popular tourist attraction in the city.

Yonghegong, popularly known as the Lama Temple, is located in the northeast part of Beijing. To its west is the famous Confucius Temple and Imperial Academy. The Lama Temple is the largest and best-preserved lamasery in Beijing which is 480 meters long and 120 meters wide, with a total area of 66,000 square meters. It is also a well-known monastery of the Gelugpa, the Yellow Sect of Tibetan Buddhism in mainland China. History The Lama Temple was originally a palatial residence built in 1694 by Qing Emperor Kangxi (1654-1722) for his fourth son, Prince Yongzheng (1678-1735), who later succeeded the throne. After the death of his father, Emperor Yongzheng moved to the Forbidden City and converted half of his former residence into a temple for the monks of Yellow sect, and the other half served as a temporary palace for him. In 1735, Emperor Yongzheng died and then his son Qianlong (1711-1799) succeeded the throne. He put his father’s coffin here for more than one year before moving it to the Western Qing Tombs, the burial ground of the emperors in the Qing Dynasty (1644 - 1911). He also upgraded Yonghegong to the status of an Imperial Palace by replacing the green titles of the roof with yellow ones, for the yellow color was the imperial color in the old days. In 1744, Yonghegong was formally converted into a lamasery. After 1949, the Chinese Government attached great importance to the Lama Temple. Several renovations have been carried out since then, and the Temple has taken on a new look. In 1950 and 1952, the government allocated large sums of money to renovate it. In 1961, the Lama Temple was listed by the State Council as a major national cultural relic and historical site under the state’s protection. During the ten-year Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976, the Lama Temple was very well preserved because of the special care given by former Premier Zhou Enlai. The latest renovation was carried out in 1976, and in 1981 the Lama Temple was reopened to the public. Today, there are rich collections of cultural relics which are preserved in the Lama Temple, especially those related to Tibetan Buddhism. For instance, there is a large number of vividly sculptured Buddhist images of various sizes, each different in posture and expression; a large collection of Tibetan-style paintings known as Tangka paintings; delicate frescoes, scriptures and religious instruments; the inscriptions and calligraphic works on the stele and boards, and Buddhist scriptures in the languages of Manchu, Tibetan, Han, Mongolian and Sanskrit, all of which being of very high cultural and historical value for the Chinese people. Presently, there are nearly 100 lamas in the Lama Temple and most of them are Mongolians, Tibetans and people from Qinghai province. Daily traditional religious ceremonies and activities in the Lama Temple are undertaken strictly according to the regulation and disciplines of Tibetan Buddhism. When people visit the Lama Temple, please pay attention to the belt that the lamas have, because the color of it reflects the rank of them. Lamas in red belts are the lowest rank of lamas in the Temple, while lamas with yellow belts are higher rank of lamas. If people see a lama in orange belt, he is probably the head lama in the Lama Temple.

雍和宮，作為北京著名的藏傳佛教寺院，擁有悠久的歷史與深厚的文化底蘊。這裡的建築風格獨特，融合了漢、藏、蒙多種民族元素，讓人印象深刻。寺內的佛像雕刻精美，香火鼎盛，是許多信眾朝拜的聖地。此外，雍和宮周邊的環境清幽，古樹參天，為遊客提供了一個寧靜的休憩場所。總體而言，雍和宮不僅是信仰的寄託，也是文化與藝術的展現，值得一遊。四星推薦，略顯遺憾的是部分區域正在維修，稍影響遊覽體驗。

雍和宮位於北京市東城區雍和宮大街，是北京最大的藏傳佛教寺院，其南北長400米，占地66000平方米，布局分為東、中、西三路，共有五進院落。其始建於明代，原為太監官房。1694年，清朝康熙皇帝在其舊址上為皇四子雍親王胤禛（即雍正皇帝）建立了府邸。雍正皇帝即位後，將其前半部改為黃教上院，後半作為行宮，後行宮遇火被焚。1725年，上院改為行宮，正式更名為雍和宮。1744年，雍和宮改為藏傳佛教寺院至今。中華人民共和國建立後，其於1957年入選第一批北京市文物保護單位，1961年成為第一批全國重點文物保護單位。

ここはやばい パワースポット 全ての欲望を叶えるお参り場所がある完璧なお寺 説明 雍和宫（Yōnghé Gōng）は北京にある著名なチベット仏教寺院で、清朝時代に建てられました。元々は清の雍正帝（Yōngzhèng）になる前の雍親王の邸宅でしたが、彼が皇帝になった後、1744年に寺院として改装されました。 雍和宮は北京で最も重要な仏教寺院の一つで、多くの仏教信者や観光客が訪れます。寺院は複数の主要な建物から構成されており、特に有名なものには雍和殿、大雄宝殿、そして万福閣にある巨大な弥勒菩薩像などがあります。この弥勒菩薩像は一本の白檀木から彫られており、ギネスブックに登録されています。 雍和宫はチベット仏教の修行や儀式が行われる場所としても重要で、歴史的・文化的価値が高い場所です。その美しい建築と静かな雰囲気は、訪れる人々に平和と敬虔な気持ちをもたらします。

🌟 雍和宮參拜心得｜歷史厚重、香火鼎盛、腳也走到快燙起水泡 🌟 一走進雍和宮，立刻感受到一種「我是不是該先肅靜一下」的氛圍。建築超有氣勢，古色古香，每個角落都很出片，走的是莊嚴美學路線。 🕯️ 香火真的旺到不行 一進去就能聞到濃濃的香氣，參拜人潮絡繹不絕。不管信仰如何，來到這裡都會自動進入「誠心許願模式」，三炷香一拜、還願默念、祈求順利全都來一套。氣氛不壓迫，但真的很靜很莊嚴，會不自覺收起平常的吵鬧感。 📿 寺內導覽牌很詳細（也推薦自備一點佛教冷知識） 有不少藏傳佛教元素，如果不是宗教迷，建議可以稍微查點資料或用語音導覽，不然看著滿滿經文跟雕像會有點「資訊量爆棚但看不懂」的空虛感。 👣 走路動線多、地磚硬派，要穿好走的鞋 從大殿走到後殿，再到大佛像那邊，一路走下來真的會覺得自己腳底板快升天（不是靈魂那種升天，是物理疲勞的那種）。拍照的點很多，但也真的是走好走滿。 📸 不能亂拍照！裡面有些地方明文禁止拍照，一定要尊重現場規定。 不然不只工作人員會來提醒，旁邊的香客也會用眼神教育你。 🧧 周邊賣平安符、開運小物的攤位也不少 價格合理，不會有那種「觀光客專屠價」的感覺，還可以當伴手禮送長輩，保平安又有文化氣息。

เป็นวัดที่พระพุทธรูปสวยมาก เป็นวัดที่ดูเหมือนจะเล็ก แต่ใหญ่มากครับ ตอนเดินเข้าไปก็งงทำไมให้ธูปมาเป็นกำมือเลย คือจะมีพระพุทธรูปหลายองค์มากครับ สามารถไหว้องค์ไหนตามที่เราต้องการได้เลย คือเดินผ่านแต่ละจุดก็มีที่ให้ไหว้ไปหมด ถ้าจะให้ดีต้องหาข้อมูลมาว่าไหว้องค์ไหนขออะไรจะดีมากครับ พระพุทธรูปแต่ละองค์สวยงดงามมากๆครับ

По китайским меркам этот храм не очень старый - стройка началась в конце 17 века. Да и храмом он сначала не был, а дворцом (здесь было что-то вроде общежития дворцовых евнухов). А евнухи в императорском Китае были очень значимой дворцовой кастой, поэтому их место жительства выглядит так пышно. Сейчас это храм тибетского буддизма, очень почитаемый у буддистов. Но и прочим гражданам тут интересно. Лично я получила большое удовольствие от рассматривания его архитектурных особенностей. Больше всего понравились удивительной красоты крыши.

YONGHE Gong is the largest Tibetan Buddhist Lama temple, which was built in 1694 as the residence of the Qing Dynasty Prince Yong. In Chinese, "YONGHE Gong" means a harmony and peace palace. The architecture and layout of this place is really incredible, the giant sandalwood carved Buddha is particularly impressive. In this temple we can see also the bronze Buddhas of past, present, and future. Worth a visit if only to enjoy the peace and tranquility, and escape the noise of modern Beijing. 近年來雍和宮因為「步步驚心」劇中的四爺拉抬了人氣，這裡就是雍正皇帝繼位前所居住的「四爺府」、「禛貝勒府」、「雍王府」，連乾隆皇帝也是在這裡誕生！此處被視作福地 。 萬福閣裡的巨大彌勒佛是雍和宮最知名的珍寶，由巨大白檀香木雕成，高十八公尺，地下還深埋了八公尺，這是第七世達賴喇嘛從尼泊爾購進一整株巨大白檀香木，由西藏經四川走水路，歷時三年運至北京，上貢乾隆皇帝，用來感謝乾隆皇帝平定了西藏郡王朱爾默特的叛亂。乾隆皇帝命匠工將巨木雕成佛像，白檀香木彌勒大佛面相莊嚴、體態宏偉，全身貼金，鑲以各式珠寶，佛面高度在樓閣的三層之上，獲得金氏世界紀錄，為獨木雕刻佛像世界之最。 當年文革期間因為周恩來總理的重視, 庸和宮得以渡過文化浩劫. 這座喇嘛黃教的建築瑰寶在1981年重新對社會大眾開放.

Юнхэгун - Дворец Мира и Гармонии или в народе «Храм Ламы». Действующий ламаистский монастырь в Пекине. Памятник архитектуры к. XVII - н. XVIII в. Первоначально строился в качестве дворца одного из сыновей самого прославленного цинского императора Канси. Расположен не далеко от восточных ворот внутреннего города. После восшествия хозяина на престол под девизом Юнчжэн, дворец частично был отдан тибетским монахам. После кончины императора в 1735 году, его тело было погребено здесь, а его наследник Цяньлун даровал храму статус императорского, повелев заменить черепицу на золотую глазурованную. Архитектура комплекса выдержана в традиционном китайском стиле с элементами тибетской и монгольской. Ансамбль простирается с юга на север по длине около полукилометра и представляет собой 5 залов разделённых дворами. В последнем зале - «павильоне 10000 удач», находится главная достопримечательность монастыря - 26-метровая статуя Будды-Майтрейи, вырезанная из огромного сандала - крупнейшая в своём роде! Монастырь дважды в своей истории избежал полного разорения и уничтожения. Примечательно, что первый раз Юнхэгун спас начальник Русской Духовной миссии архимандрит Иннокентий, которого монахи приютили в дни кровавого восстания Ихэтуаней. Второй раз монастырь удалось отстоять в годы чудовищной «Культурной Революции» вмешательством лично премьера Чжоу Энлая. Юнхэгун нельзя назвать очень популярным туристическим местом, большинство людей, которых вы здесь встретите - верующие, пришедшие в храм помолиться. Добраться сюда несложно: вам потребуется одноименная станция кольцевой-синей или 5-й фиолетовой ветки. С кольцевой ветки идите к выходу “C”, юго-запад, впрочем указатели везде есть. Проезжая по шоссе Андинмэн’ храм хорошо виден, ночью он не подсвечивается... Тёмная громада павильона «Ван’фугэ» практически примыкает к шоссе и хорошо видна на фоне ночного неба.

El Templo de Yonghe o, más conocido como el Templo de los Lamas de Pekín (Lama Temple), es uno de los lugares de interés principales de esta ciudad. Habitualmente recibe gran cantidad de visitantes, religiosos y/o turistas. La visita es amena y fácil, ya que la estructura típica de este tipo de complejos permite ir pasando a través de los edificios en orden hasta llegar al más alejado (el que, normalmente, es el más importante). La duración aproximada de la visita es de 1 hora, a no ser que tengas una devoción especial por este tipo de lugares y quieras quedarte a rezar o a leer toda la información de cada estructura. Como es habitual en los templos budistas, hay incienso por todas partes, lo que dota al espacio de un clima relajado y propicio para la reflexión.

北京最大のチベット仏教寺院。万福閣の弥勒菩薩像は1本の白檀の巨木から彫りだされ、高さ26m(地上18m 地下8m)・直径8m・重さ約100tで木製仏像として中国最大、ギネス認定も受けている。 いくつかの建物内で仏像や仏具の展示があるが撮影は禁止されている。 チベット仏教といえばマニ車(中に経典が入っている円筒状の道具で、一周回すと一回経典を読んだことになるチートアイテム)が有名だが、この辺の仏具店(お土産屋？)には太陽電池で回り続けるソーラーマニ車なるものが売っていた。当然おみやげに購入して車のダッシュボードに設置している。 雍和宮は、地鉄2号線5号線 雍和宮駅のすぐ南東にある。北には『地壇公園』、西には『五道営胡同』『孔子廟・国子監』『方家胡同46号』などがある。

Es mag überraschen, in Peking auf einen tibetisch-buddhistischen Tempel zu stossen. Allerdings hat dies keinen politischen Nebengeschmack, wie man im ersten Moment vermuten könnte. Der Yonghe-Tempel, Palast des Friedens und der Harmonie, ist die ehemalige Residenz des Prinzen Yinzhen, welche 1744 unter Kaiser Qiánlóng zu Ehren seines Vaters in einen Tempel der tibetischen Tradition umbauen liess. Umgangssprachlich wird er auch Lamatempel genannt, was jedoch irreführend ist, da das Wort Lama sich einzig auf die Person des Mönchs bezieht, der tibetische Buddhismus mit seinen vier Ausrichtungen jedoch nicht so benennt werden kann. Also "Lamaismus" eine laienhafte Fehlbezeichnung darstellt. Es ist einer der grössten Tempel der tibetischen Tradition ausserhalb Tibets und ist in einwandfreiem Zustand. Die Anlage verfügt über einen Ziergarten, mehrere Innenhöfe und veschiedene Hallen. Der 7. Dalai Lama, Kelsong Gyatsho (1708 - 1757), schenkte dem Tempel eine aus Sandelholz geschnitzte Statue des Bodisattva Maitreya, die 18 m hoch und aus einem Stamm erstellt wurde. Als Bodhisattva gilt im Mahayana-Buddhismus ein Erleuchteter, der den Übergang ins Nirvana zurückgestellt hat, um weiterhin den leidenden Menschen beizustehen. In China nennt man sie Kwan Yin. 雍和宫(The Lama Temple)位于北京市区东北角，清康熙三十三年(1694年)，康熙帝在此建造府邸、赐予四子雍亲王，称雍亲王府。 雍正三年(1725年)，改王府为行宫，称雍和宫。雍正十三年(1735年)，雍正驾崩，曾于此停放灵柩，因此，雍和宫主要殿堂原绿色琉璃瓦改为黄色琉璃瓦。又因乾隆皇帝诞生于此，雍和宫出了两位皇帝，成了“龙潜福地”，所以殿宇为黄瓦红墙，与紫禁城皇宫一样规格。乾隆九年(1744年)，雍和宫改为-庙，特派总理事务王大臣管理本宫事务，无定员。可以说，雍和宫是全国规格最高的一座佛教寺院。雍和宫由和天王殿、雍和宫大殿(大雄宝殿)、永佑殿、0殿、万福阁等五进宏伟大殿组成，另外还有东西配殿、“四学殿”(讲经殿、密宗殿、数学殿、药师殿)。整个建筑布局院落从南向北渐次缩小，而殿宇则依次升高。形成“正殿高大而重院深藏”的格局，巍峨壮观，具有汉、满、蒙、藏民族的特色。

A Jungho templom vagy Láma templom egy templom és a tibeti buddhista gelug iskola monostora, mely Peking északkeleti részén található. Ez az egyik legnagyobb és legjelentősebb tibeti buddhista monostor a világon. Az építmény és a templomi alkotások a han kínai és a tibeti stílus kombinációi. A Láma Templom az egyetlen működő tibeti buddhista kolostor Peking területén. Mindegy, hogy télen, vagy nyáron látogatjuk, számítani kell a tömegre, de ha van rá lehetőség, akkor hétköznap délelőtt elkerülhetjük a sorbanállást. Miután egy működő kolostorról van szó, ezért ha nem is mély, de valamilyen szintű betekintést nyerhetünk az egyébként elzártan működő kolostorok életébe, anélkül, hogy Tibetbe kellene hozzá utaznunk. A templom építése 1694-ben, a Csing-dinasztia idején kezdődött. Eredetileg eunuchok számára készült, később Kang-hszi császár fiának, Jung hercegnek (később Jung-cseng császár) lett átalakítva. Amikor 1722-ben Jung-cseng a trónra került, az épület felét lámakolostorrá alakították át tibeti buddhista szerzetesek részére, a másik fele császári palota maradt. 1735-ben Jung-cseng halála után koporsóját a templomban helyezték el. Csien-lung kínai császár, Jung-cseng utódja császári státuszt adott a templomnak, melyet azzal jelöltek, hogy türkiz csempéit sárgára cserélték le, ami a császár számára volt fenntartva. Ezután a monostort nagy számban lakták Mongóliából és Tibetből érkező tibeti buddhista szerzetesek, így a Jungho láma templom a láma közigazgatás nemzeti központjává vált. 1949-ben a kínai polgárháború idején a templomot bezárták és műemlékké nyilvánították.
